title: Subsets
prompt:
Given an array of distinct numbers, return every subset (also called the power set), including the empty subset and the full array. The order of subsets, and the order inside each subset, does not matter.

Write subsets(nums).

subsets([1, 2, 3]);
// [[], [1], [1,2], [1,2,3], [1,3], [2], [2,3], [3]]   (8 subsets, any order)

Constraints: nums.length is 0 to 10 (so at most 210 = 1,024 subsets). All numbers are different.

tests.name: [1,2,3] has 8 subsets
tests.code:
function norm(lists) { return lists.map((l) => [...l].sort((a, b) => a - b)).map((l) => JSON.stringify(l)).sort(); }
assertEqual(norm(subsets([1,2,3])), norm([[],[1],[2],[3],[1,2],[1,3],[2,3],[1,2,3]]));

tests.name: empty input has exactly one subset: the empty one
single element
tests.code:
function norm(lists) { return lists.map((l) => [...l].sort((a, b) => a - b)).map((l) => JSON.stringify(l)).sort(); }
assertEqual(norm(subsets([7])), norm([[],[7]]));

tests.name: works with negatives and zero
tests.code:
function norm(lists) { return lists.map((l) => [...l].sort((a, b) => a - b)).map((l) => JSON.stringify(l)).sort(); }
assertEqual(norm(subsets([-1,0,5])), norm([[],[-1],[0],[5],[-1,0],[-1,5],[0,5],[-1,0,5]]));

tests.name: 10 numbers give 1,024 distinct subsets
subsets are independent copies (no shared array)

hints: Trigger: "all subsets", "all combinations", "every possible", with a tiny input size (n ≤ 10 to 20). Listing everything means exponential output, so backtracking is the tool.

Idea: walk a decision tree. current holds the numbers chosen so far. Every node in the tree is a valid subset, so save it on entry. Then try adding each remaining number (only ones to the right of the last choice, so [1,2] and [2,1] are not both produced).

Code shape: result.push([...current]); for (let i = start; i < nums.length; i++) { current.push(nums[i]); explore(i + 1); current.pop(); }. The copy [...current] matters: pushing current itself stores the same array 8 times, and it ends up empty.
explain:
Time O(n × 2n): there are 2n subsets and copying each costs up to n. Space O(n) for the recursion and current, not counting the output. You can't beat 2n because the answer itself has 2n items.

Say it: "Each number is either in or out, so there are 2 to the n subsets. I'll backtrack: choose a number, recurse on the numbers after it, then undo the choice. Every node of the decision tree is a subset, so I record a copy on entry."
